# In Praise of Boring Inventions

Some inventions get statues and biographies: the printing press, the telephone, the lightbulb. But I keep coming back to the ones nobody celebrates, the ones so well-designed that they've become invisible.

Take the **zipper**. It's two rows of tiny interlocking teeth and a slider that wedges them together or pries them apart. The principle is strange when you think about it: a wedge shape, repeated dozens of times, turns a single motion into a secure seam. Yet you probably haven't marveled at a zipper since childhood, when you couldn't work one.

Or the **index at the back of a book**. It's a second, alternate way through the text, built by someone who had to read the whole thing sideways, asking not "what happens next?" but "where does everything live?" An index turns a linear experience into a searchable one. It's a small act of generosity toward a reader you'll never meet, who has a specific question and not much time.

Or the **calendar week**. Seven days has no astronomical justification. The day, month, and year are tied to the sun and moon, but the week is pure human agreement, a rhythm we invented and then organized our lives around. Nobody owns it, nobody enforces it, and it has survived for millennia because it works.

What these have in common is that their success is measured by how little you think about them. A great zipper is one you forget. A great index is one you use in ten seconds and never remember using. Their genius is in removing friction, and friction removed leaves no trace.

I find that a little moving. So much of what makes life livable is made of quiet decisions by people who were trying to solve small problems well: the person who decided that stairs should have uniform step heights, the person who put a raised dot on the F and J keys, the person who first thought to put a handle on a cup. None of them got a parade, but each one made thousands of small moments slightly smoother.

It makes me suspect that a lot of what we call progress is less about breakthroughs and more about accumulated tidiness, about many people, over many years, sanding the rough edges off the world.

And it suggests a modest way to live: notice the things that work. Occasionally thank the invisible design. And if you ever get the chance, make something so useful that people forget it was ever made.
